name: Ember US monthly electricity — demand & generation (TWh) with HDD/CDD, population, industrial production & clean share — US monthly electricity demand (long-term capacity planning) (covariate forecasting bundle)
citation: Ember — monthly full release (https://storage.googleapis.com/emb-prod-bkt-publicdata/public-downloads/monthly_full_release_long_format.csv); Open-Meteo Historical Weather API (https://archive-api.open-meteo.com/v1/archive); World Bank Open Data API — indicator SP.POP.TOTL (https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/USA/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL?format=json&per_page=100); FRED (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=INDPRO)
license: Ember: CC-BY 4.0. Open-Meteo: CC-BY 4.0. World Bank Open Data: CC-BY 4.0. FRED/INDPRO: underlying Federal Reserve Board series is US-government public domain; redistributed via FRED.
description: US monthly electricity demand (long-term capacity planning). This bundle forecasts `us_electricity_demand` from a covariate panel of heating_degree_days, cooling_degree_days, us_population, industrial_production_index, month_of_year, clean_electricity_share. Source dataset 'Ember US monthly electricity — demand & generation (TWh) with HDD/CDD, population, industrial production & clean share' — monthly cadence, 137 rows, 2015-01-01..2026-05-01. NON-EIA (the forecasting model is trained on EIA data, so EIA inputs are excluded): NONE of these are EIA. Ember is an independent global energy think-tank compiling its own monthly electricity dataset. Open-Meteo weather is ERA5 reanalysis from ECMWF/Copernicus. Population is World Bank; industrial production is the Federal Reserve Board's INDPRO via FRED. No series is sourced from or derived from eia.gov.
preprocessing: 1. Download Ember 'monthly_full_release_long_format.csv' from the public GCS bucket (cached under datasets/raw/).
2. Filter to ISO 3 code == 'USA'. Parse 'Date' (first-of-month) into 'month'.

3. Extract three long-format series into wide columns: (Category='Electricity demand', Variable='Demand', Unit='TWh')->demand_twh; (Category='Electricity generation', Variable='Total Generation', Unit='TWh')->generation_twh; (Category='Electricity generation', Variable='Clean', Unit='%')->clean_share_pct.
4. Build the monthly target index 2015-01-01 .. 2026-05-01 (MS) and left-join the Ember columns onto it.

5. Pull Open-Meteo ERA5 daily mean temperature for 12 large US metros (2015-01-01 .. 2026-05-31). Per metro per day compute HDD=max(0,18-T) and CDD=max(0,T-18), weight by metro population, sum across metros -> daily population-weighted HDD/CDD; resample to monthly sums.

6. Fetch World Bank SP.POP.TOTL annual US population; anchor each annual value at mid-year (year+0.5) and linearly interpolate to each month's decimal year; linearly extrapolate the months beyond the last annual point (2025).
7. Fetch FRED INDPRO industrial production CSV; parse to monthly and join on 'month'.
9. Assert demand_twh (target) is complete and no NaNs remain across the window; write wide CSV sorted by month. Last 12 months (2025-06 .. 2026-05) are the evaluation holdout and all have actuals.
10. Dropped calendar/time-derived variables (month_of_year) so the only notion of time retained is the shared timestamps list.

11. Renamed all variable names and units from snake_case codes to plain English (CSV row/column structure unchanged). Name and unit mapping — us_electricity_demand [TWh] -> "US electricity demand" [terawatt-hours] (target; US monthly total electricity demand); heating_degree_days [°C·day] -> "heating degree days" [degree-days Celsius] (covariate; heating degree-days); cooling_degree_days [°C·day] -> "cooling degree days" [degree-days Celsius] (covariate; cooling degree-days); us_population [persons] -> "US population" [persons] (covariate; US total population (linearly interpolated to month)); industrial_production_index [index (2017=100)] -> "industrial production index" [index (2017=100)] (covariate; US industrial production index (FRED INDPRO, 2017=100)); clean_electricity_share [%] -> "clean electricity share" [percent] (covariate; clean (low-carbon) share of US electricity generation).
